Double tip and tail

Light going both ways round a ring (paper, Example 12.2). The forward and backward beams span one pair: the pair is the tail, the mode inside it is the tip. Rotation splits the two directions; scattering couples them.

Below lock-in the two directions act as one: the pattern stands still and only the pair can be read. Above it the beams run at different frequencies, the pattern slides at the beat, and each direction is a tip you can measure. Moving both mirrors together only slides the pattern; the pair holds either way.

Two mirrors, two tips

Two tip-and-tail systems face each other. Each surface is a tail: the plane of its two lower levels, held by its outer gap. Each tip is the single lowest direction, held only by the small inner gap. A's tip lands on B's surface and pushes B's levels; B's tip lands on A's and pushes back.

Mirrors
Readout
A: tip turned
A: tail tilted
B: tip turned
B: tail tilted
separation
coupling felt

Only A is pushed. With the coupling at zero, B's tip stays still. Raise it and B's tip starts answering A's through the light line, and A's tip feels B's answer. The two surfaces barely move either way: the outer gaps hold the tails while the tips trade motion. Narrow the outer gap and the surfaces start to tilt as well.

Every number on this page is computed live in your browser from the formulas of the paper, except the condensate tables and eigen-images 2 and 3, which are measured: the NIST dark-soliton analysis (odd/even and two random splits). The core was checked before publishing against the paper: turning points 0.32981248 and −1.0969, swap/cycle lengths 3.512 and 2.896, speed under its ceiling, curvature inside its envelope, the Fisher speed equal to the metric speed, two-level and spin-1 bands on the bound and generic three-level bands inside it.
